title: Applications of Vectors — Work, Torque, Angular Momentum
topicTitle: Applications of Vectors — Work, Torque, Angular Momentum
notes: 1. Work Done by a Force
When a constant force F acts on an object and displaces it by d, the work done is:
W = F · d = |F| |d| cos θ
where θ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
Key insight: Only the component of force in the direction of displacement does work. If force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°), no work is done.
Examples:
(a) Lifting a box vertically: W = |F| |d| (θ = 0°, cos 0° = 1)
(b) Carrying a box horizontally: W = 0 (θ = 90°, the force is vertical but displacement is horizontal)
(c) Pulling a sled at an angle: W = |F| |d| cos θ, where θ is the angle of the pull above horizontal
2. Torque (Moment of Force)
Torque measures the turning effect of a force about a point or axis:
τ = r × F
where r is the position vector from the pivot point to the point of force application, and F is the force vector.
Magnitude: |τ| = |r| |F| sin θ = |F| × (perpendicular distance from pivot)
Direction: Perpendicular to the plane of r and F (right-hand rule). The direction indicates the axis of rotation.
Key insight: Maximum torque occurs when the force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm (θ = 90°). Pushing directly toward or away from the pivot gives zero torque.
3. Angular Momentum
Angular momentum of a particle about a point is defined as:
L = r × p = r × (mv)
where r is the position vector from the origin to the particle, and p = mv is the linear momentum.
Magnitude: |L| = m|r| |v| sin θ = mvd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line of motion.
Conservation: If the net torque on a system is zero, angular momentum is conserved: L = constant.
Example: A planet orbiting the sun has constant angular momentum because the gravitational force is central (always directed toward the sun).
4. Applications Summary
Dot product applications: Work (W = F · d), power (P = F · v), component of a vector.
Cross product applications: Torque (τ = r × F), angular momentum (L = r × p), magnetic force (F = qv × B).
Scalar triple product applications: Volume of parallelepiped, coplanarity check, volume of tetrahedron.
5. Right-Hand Rule in Physics
The right-hand rule is essential for determining the direction of cross product results:
Torque: Point fingers along r, curl toward F; thumb gives direction of τ.
Angular momentum: Point fingers along r, curl toward v; thumb gives direction of L.
Magnetic force: Point fingers along v, curl toward B; thumb gives direction of F (for positive charge).
6. Equilibrium Conditions
Translational equilibrium: The net force is zero: ΣF = 0.
Rotational equilibrium: The net torque about any point is zero: Στ = 0.
Both conditions must be satisfied for a rigid body to be in complete static equilibrium.
7. Power as a Dot Product
The instantaneous power delivered by a force is the rate at which work is done:
P = dW/dt = F · v = |F| |v| cos θ
where v is the velocity of the point of application of the force.
8. Moment of a Force About a Line
The moment of a force F about an axis (line) with unit direction vector u is:
M = u · (r × F)
This gives the scalar component of torque along the specified axis.
confusion: Work is a scalar (dot product), while torque is a vector (cross product). Do not confuse W = F · d with τ = r × F.
In torque τ = r × F, the vector r must start from the pivot point. Using the wrong point gives wrong torque.
Angular momentum L = r × p depends on the choice of origin. Different origins give different angular momenta, but the change is meaningful in physics.
If a force passes through the pivot point (collinear with r), the torque is zero — the force produces no rotation. This is because sin 0° = 0.
Power = F · v (dot product) gives the rate of doing work. It is NOT F × v (cross product), which would give a vector with no physical meaning in this context.
Work can be negative when the force opposes the displacement (θ > 90°), but torque magnitude is always non-negative when computed as |r||F|sin θ.
practice: A force F = 3i + 4j N acts on an object that moves from (1, 2) to (5, 8) m. Find the work done.
A force F = 2i − j + 3k N is applied at point P(1, 2, 3) m. Find the torque about the origin.
A particle of mass 2 kg moves with velocity v = 3i + 4j m/s at position r = 2i − j + k m. Find its angular momentum about the origin.
A wrench of length 0.3 m is used to tighten a bolt. If a force of 50 N is applied perpendicular to the wrench, find the torque.
A 5 N force is applied at a 30° angle to a displacement of 4 m. Find the work done.
A force F = 4i − 3j + 2k N acts at point (1, 2, 3). Find the moment about the point (2, 0, 1).
universalFacts: Work is measured in Joules (J) = Newton-meter (N⋅m). While torque also has units of N⋅m, work is scalar while torque is vector.
Angular momentum is conserved in any system with no external torque. This explains why ice skaters spin faster when they pull in their arms.
The dot product F · d extracts the component of force along the displacement. The cross product r × F extracts the perpendicular component that causes rotation.
In all three applications (work, torque, angular momentum), the vector operation (dot or cross) is chosen based on what physical quantity is being measured — scalar vs. vector.
The conservation of angular momentum explains why a spinning top remains upright and why planets orbit in fixed planes.
